name: Kara
confidence_why: Kara (Cara/Caranqui) is extinct and known only from colonial place and personal names, and the one remark on its stress is a footnote by the ethnohistorian Caillavet (2000) inferring final stress from the single toponym Piguchí, while Adelaar and Muysken (2004) and Montaluisa (2018) say nothing about its accent and Caillavet herself states that nothing is known of the language.

new_statements.translation: Piguchí: stressed on the final syllable. An oxytone word belonging to the pre-Inca language of the area. The present-day stress on the penultimate syllable, Peguche, is without any doubt due to the influence exerted by the Quechua language.

The note is keyed to 'una estancia en el desaguadero de este di…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accentual remark found: a native (pre-Inca, i.e. Cara/Otavalo-language) toponym carried final-syllable stress, and penultimate stress in its modern form is a later Quechua overlay. By implication (and consistent with the many Cara toponymic endings written with final accent: -quí, -bí/-pí, -chí, e.g. Cochasquí, Pomasquí, Tuntaquí, Cahuasquí), Cara words/place names were oxytone. This is an ethnohistorian's footnote about onomastic material, not a phonological description; the language itself is unattested beyond toponyms and personal names.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the note itself records that the modern Quechua-ised form Peguche has penultimate stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Applies to a colonial-era toponym (citation/orthographic form in a 1609 Spanish document); evidence base for the language is exclusively toponyms and anthroponyms, so 'word stress' here means the accentuation of recorded place names. No first-hand phonological description of Kara exists or can exist (extinct by 18th c., no texts).
new_statements.identity_note: Caillavet refers to 'el idioma preincaico de la zona' / 'la lengua otavalo' spoken from Quito to the Chota-Mira river, i.e. the Cara/Caranqui language = Glottolog kara1506 'Kara' (name after Paz y Mino 1941). Not to be confused with Cara (Teriya) of Nigeria (en-Wikipedia 'Cara language'). The statement concerns a single Otavalo-area toponym (Piguchi'/Peguche); the language is known only from toponyms and anthroponyms.

sources.note: Ch. IV-3 p. 470 n. 3: the toponym Piguchi' (modern Peguche, Otavalo) is stressed on the final syllable, 'palabra aguda propia del idioma preincaico de la zona'; the modern penultimate stress is attributed to Quechua influence. Ch. I-5 (Toponimia historica, pp. 103-107) discusses i/e, o/u and voicing variation in colonial spellings of the aboriginal language but nothing further on accent. Only accent remark in the book (a full-text search for stress/accent).
